idiom_name: dynamic import() type-checked by the compiler; runtime module resolution as lookup service
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds no runtime lookup machinery - the host runtime's module resolver performs name-to-location resolution for import(specifier), and the compiler type-checks the resolved shape, so a misbinding of a static specifier is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise; ambient module declarations describe runtime-provided modules (such as the Node built-ins) that have no corresponding file. What replaces the classic structure is static typing plus, for genuinely dynamic names, a small typed registry: a Record<string, () => Promise<T>> keeps the legal names explicit and turns a miss into an explicit error. Runtime cache semantics are JavaScript's: one module instance per specifier, no invalidation API.
pitfalls: A computed specifier (import(`./renderers/${name}.js`)) defeats both type checking and the bundler's static analysis; keep the literal mapping table and validate names against it.
Type-only imports (import type) are erased at emit, so using such a binding in a value position compiles but fails at runtime.
Module instances are cached per specifier and cannot be invalidated, so reloading needs the query-parameter trick, which leaks the previous instance.
